I used to think ignoring my feelings meant I was mature. 

Now I treat emotions as basic signals that tell me what I actually care about.

Paying attention to them is how you grow.

Judge Caprio actually took the time to understand this man's situation.

We all have rules at work, but we still need to use our own judgment.

Good managers know when to ignore the rulebook and treat people like human beings.

Talking to kids about online safety is hard. 

This campaign uses humor to talk to them instead of just scaring them. 

Ask questions, be honest, and stay involved to keep them safe online.

When microservices fail in production.

One service goes down.

Then the next.

Then the next.

Keep your blast radius small.

Explaining sorting algorithms to non-technical stakeholders.

Sometimes a visual is worth 1000 words.

No slides. No jargon. Just bars moving.

Reading legacy documentation.

The docs say one thing.

The code does another.

The only source of truth is the code itself.

Algorithmic efficiency, visualized.

Watch Bubble Sort struggle.

Then watch Quick Sort finish in a fraction of the time.

There is a reason we pick the right tool.

Business logic vs edge cases.

Your code handles 99% of inputs perfectly.

Users will always find the 1% you missed.

Design for failure.

When product asks for a "simple feature".

The underlying architecture rarely agrees.

Nothing is simple once you look under the hood.

The most important skill for a senior engineer is not knowing the answer.

It is knowing exactly how to find it.

When leadership decides to "help out" with a little code cleanup right before the release.

Please. Stop. Helping.

Open source in a nutshell.

We all build on work done by someone else.

Who probably copied it from a forum post in 2012.

A one week unpaid trial is not a trial.

It is free labor.

This person declined the offer in one line.

No apology. No explanation. Just a clear boundary.

Know your worth before someone else sets it for you.

We have all been Bryson at some point.

Watch till the end.

Stomach rumbled during a job interview.

The interviewer asked if I forgot lunch.

Told him no. Just hungry for success.

Sometimes confidence is all you need.

The moment you realize what life looks like for people who know nothing about AI, politics, or the economy.

Ignorance really is bliss sometimes.

Meanwhile the rest of us are refreshing feeds at 2am.

How badly do you want it?

Because talk is cheap.

Everyone has goals.

Few have discipline.

Stop making excuses. Start making progress.

Humans: spend 6 hours building something in AI.

AI: "Impressive. Keep going, human."

We are literally training our own replacements.

And feeling proud about it.

You spend 3 days debugging.

Finally fix it.

Feel like a genius.

Then remember ChatGPT could have done it in 4 seconds.

Proud moment and existential crisis at the same time.

When AI hits its rate limit mid-conversation.

You were so close to the answer.

Now you wait.

The most frustrating loading screen of our generation.

New AI tool every week.

New framework every month.

New paradigm every quarter.

Remember when learning one skill was enough for a decade?

Now it barely lasts a quarter.

Your employees are pasting company data into ChatGPT right now.

No policy. No oversight. No audit trail.

Shadow AI is not a future problem.

It is happening today in every company that has not set boundaries.

When the CEO says "we have no plans for layoffs."

Two weeks later: restructuring.

Always watch what they do.

Never just what they say.

The AI timeline so far:

2022: ChatGPT launches.
2023: Everyone becomes a prompt engineer.
2024: AI replaces junior devs.
2025: AI agents run workflows.
2026: You report to an AI manager.

Seven years. Too many canon events.

The moment you realize you have been arguing with a human when ChatGPT would have agreed with you instantly.

We are training ourselves to prefer AI conversations over human ones.

That should concern all of us.

Raoul Pal said it clearly.

Knowledge is approaching zero value.

Anyone can ask AI the same question you spent 10 years learning to answer.

The advantage now is judgment, taste, and the ability to ask the right questions.

Sam Altman thinks one person with a laptop can build a billion dollar company.

No co-founders. No employees. Just AI tools.

We are closer to this than most people realize.

The question is not if. It is who does it first.

When you ask AI to write your resignation letter and it writes it better than anything you have ever written.

The tool you used to quit is better at your job than you are.

Let that sink in.

Micromanagers buy physical presence. Leaders buy outcomes.

If your team has to explain why they are late for a doctor's appointment or why they need to work from home, you have infantilized your workplace.

If they deliver results and keep clients happy, their physical location or exact hours shouldn't matter.

We are dealing with adults. Stop watching the clock. Focus on output.

Ageism in tech is a massive arbitrage opportunity.

Companies filter out applicants over 50 using "culture fit" or "overqualified" as excuses to cut costs. In doing so, they lose decades of actual troubleshooting experience.

You can't Google institutional knowledge or crisis management.

If you want top-tier talent, stop screening for youth. Look for capability and experience.

Recruiting pipelines optimize for compliance and call it professionalism.

But the best hires are rarely perfect on paper. They have drive, resilience, and grit, which standard HR checklists fail to measure.

If a candidate shows extreme effort and hunger to deliver, that outweighs a minor schedule slip or a messy resume.

If you want top performers, stop looking for perfection. Focus on potential.

A resume gap is not a competence gap. Life happens.

Most automated recruiting tools filter out excellent candidates because of arbitrary career breaks. But resumes don't perform work. People do.

If someone has the technical skills and the right drive, their timeline doesn't matter.

Focus on the candidate, not the gap.

Abuse is not the price of high performance.

Toxic cultures promote toxic people because they hit short-term numbers. But healthy cultures understand that undermining others is a net negative.

If your "top performer" destroys team cohesion, they are actually costing the business money.

True performance is built on mutual trust, not fear.

Counting minutes destroys discretionary effort.

If a manager writes up an employee for arriving 10 minutes late, they shouldn't expect that employee to stay late when a project is failing.

You cannot command loyalty. If you treat work as a strict transaction, your team will do the same.

Net worth and job titles are lagging indicators of privilege, not leading indicators of intelligence or work ethic.

The systems keeping our society running are built by people who rarely get equity or high-paying titles.

Never confuse a prestige title with actual systemic utility. Honest work is honest.

In 1994, Bill Gates sat on 330,000 sheets of paper to demonstrate a single CD-ROM's storage capacity.

Today, a 2-million token context window holds the equivalent of four of those CD-ROMs in active LLM memory.

We went from physical distribution constraints to real-time cognitive synthesis in 30 years.

The scale of intelligence is outpacing the scale of data.

Expecting employees to work with the passion of a founder is a delusion.

They don't have your equity. They don't have your upside. It is your business, not theirs.

Pay people fairly, trust them, and align incentives. Don't expect founder effort for salary compensation.

Lowballing candidates in salary negotiations is a net-negative strategy.

Squeezing a hire below their market worth might look like a cost-saving win on HR's spreadsheet.

But they will leave the moment they see the pay disparity. The rehiring, training, and performance gap costs will dwarf the initial savings.

If you want to retain top talent, pay them what they are worth.

I mapped the entire AI agent infrastructure market. 75+ companies, $14B+ in disclosed funding, 8 infrastructure layers.

Most of the money is going to 2 layers. Bigger platforms are slowly absorbing the other 6.

Read the full analysis and see the complete market map.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

AI agents don't run on model APIs alone. They need a full infrastructure stack.

Each of the 8 layers has distinct buyers, pricing, and failure modes.

Compute → Memory → Sandboxed Execution → Perception → Orchestration → Evaluation → Security → Agents as Products

Check the full breakdown of the taxonomy.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

Compute and vertical agent products capture over 85% of total capital in this market.

Cerebras went public at a $95B market cap. Together AI crossed $1B ARR. Modal raised $466M.

The 6 middle layers split the remaining 15% among themselves.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

Bigger platforms are absorbing observability, security, and vector databases.

ClickHouse bought Langfuse. Mintlify bought Helicone. Cisco bought two security companies in 18 months.

LLM observability may not survive as a standalone category.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

Every time OpenAI or Anthropic ships a native feature, a cohort of startups loses its value proposition.

Function calling, code execution, web browsing. Each one killed several companies.

The survivors own infrastructure that model providers are unlikely to replicate.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

Agent memory is the least solved layer in the stack.

Academic research identifies 4 types. These are episodic, semantic, working, and procedural. No commercial product addresses all four well.

Vector DB funding stalled in 2023. General-purpose databases are eating their lunch.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

Sandboxed execution is one of the most defensible layers.

E2B raised $32M and runs untrusted, LLM-generated code in isolated micro-VMs. 88% of Fortune 100 use it.

Running AI-generated code on production servers is an obvious security risk. Sandboxes solve that.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

8 acquisitions happened in agent infrastructure between Sep 2024 and May 2026.

None of these acquirers built comparable capabilities in-house. Cisco, Check Point, IBM, Meta. Each chose to buy.

Incumbents missed the initial wave and chose to acquire instead.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

Incumbents acquire security and observability startups. Compute and perception tend to stay independent.

Wafer-scale chip company Cerebras or $1B ARR inference platform Together AI doesn't fold into an existing product line.

Technical depth creates staying power.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

Vercel and Cloudflare are absorbing agent infrastructure functions as platform features.

Vercel Marketplace has 22 categories. Cloudflare Workers AI runs 50+ models across 300+ edge points.

This may compress the middle layers faster than the AWS precedent suggests.

veda.ng/agent-infrastructure-stack

5 open questions the data alone can't resolve.

Do the 8 layers collapse into 3-4 bundles?
Do wrapper startups die in the next wave of model updates?
Does compute scarcity stay permanent?
Can open protocols prevent lock-in?
Who bears liability when an agent signs a contract?
